components.text: The inference does not independently establish theism because non-theistic theories may reject its explanatory premise and require holistic comparison.
Unexplained fundamental limits may count as a theoretical cost without showing that a non-theistic foundation is untenable.
Whether the limits premises independently warrant the motion-level movement from a foundation to theism or relevant perfection.
Whether unexplained foundational limits remain a genuine theoretical cost within an otherwise successful non-theistic theory.
The limits argument can retain evidential value as a comparative theoretical cost even when it does not demonstrate that a rival worldview is false.
Whether the limits argument retains evidential value when worldviews must be evaluated holistically rather than by one premise alone.
Apparently irrelevant differences among possible limits provide a specific reason to seek explanation, not merely a demand for deductive worldview rejection.
Whether there is a specific reason, beyond merely assuming a worldview, to count a particular fundamental limit as needing explanation.
A track record of successful explanation supports only a defeasible default, so background theoretical evidence can justify exceptions.
The general norm favoring reduced foundational arbitrariness cannot be treated as exceptionless merely from explanatory experience.
Whether explanatory experience and the search for deeper accounts warrant an exceptionless or strongly presumptive demand at the foundation.
Whether the proposed anti-arbitrariness strategy permits rational exceptions when independent background theory supports them.
The same inductive and relevant-difference support can motivate rival causal principles whose consequences conflict with traditional theism.
Comparative use requires accounting for similarly supported rival principles rather than counting only the limits principle's preferred cost.
Whether the offered inductive, abductive, intuitive, and relevant-difference supports uniquely favor the limits principle.
Whether the anti-arbitrariness methodology has discriminatory force when similarly supported causal principles oppose theism.
Equally supported competing principles would undercut the original argument, so their principles and supporting grounds must be compared for a symmetry breaker.
The required comparison is acknowledged as part of the broader holistic assessment rather than dismissed as irrelevant.
Competing forms of support must be examined before the explanatory default can carry distinctive force.
Whether competing, similarly supported principles undercut the original limits principle absent a symmetry breaker.
The ascent to perfection cannot begin merely from fundamentality because a mindless foundation may be axiologically neutral rather than great.
Reducing arbitrariness does not by itself supply the positive value needed for the later perfection inference.
Neutral non-theistic foundations remain live comparative options unless the greatness premise receives independent support.
Whether a fundamental reality has any initial greatness from which the argument can ascend toward relevant perfection.
Fundamental mentality arguments and the value of original value-producing power provide independent routes to some foundational greatness.
These independent routes are offered as supplementary considerations within a broader theory comparison.
Whether an apparently impersonal foundation can nevertheless possess a value-conferring feature sufficient for initial greatness.
The limits argument alone does not establish a minded foundation; reaching theism requires an additional independently supported mentality premise.
Perfection in a broad relevant sense does not by itself yield the minded divine conclusion associated with theism.
At most the limits argument supplies a comparative consideration unless an independent mindedness bridge is appended.
Whether the limits argument itself establishes mentality or instead depends on separate arguments that the foundation is minded.
Whether the route reaches a theistic or divine conclusion without an additional independently supported mindedness premise.
Even without first establishing mindedness, a value-entailing derivative reality must ultimately depend on a ground with valuable potential.
A wholly valueless foundation allegedly could not generate positive aspects because the relevant potential would itself be valuable.
Whether a wholly valueless fundamental ground can account for positive derivative aspects without itself possessing valuable potential.
Whether a value route independent of mindedness can supply some foundational greatness.
Necessary enablement of value does not entail being valuable, as necessary truths condition every valuable state without thereby acquiring value.
The same distinction challenges the inference from possessing value-producing power to being valuable.
Whether being a necessary enabling condition for valuable states suffices to make that condition valuable.
Even if a foundation has value, its nonmaximal degree may be explained by metaphysical necessity or by what that foundation essentially is.
Explained nonmaximal greatness blocks the inference from some greatness to perfection without treating the limit as unexplained.
An essentialist or necessitarian explanation supplies a relevant difference rather than leaving the selected limit brute.
Whether a nonmaximal degree of foundational greatness must remain arbitrary once the degree is metaphysically necessary or essential.
A uniquely necessitating ground of an arbitrary property inherits its arbitrariness, so necessity or essence cannot simply hide the original limit.
The move shifts from value transmission to the distinct claim that uniquely necessitating grounds inherit explanatory arbitrariness.
It does not independently show that the foundation possesses initial greatness or value.
Whether necessity or essence genuinely explains a nonmaximal limit without relocating the same arbitrariness into its uniquely necessitating ground.
General inheritance threatens to make God inherit created limits, while a grounding-only restriction needs justification given grounding's explanatory role.
The challenge also pressures broad transmission principles from derivative features to their grounds.
A divine explanation of limited creation must remain compatible with the route's claim to an arbitrariness-free perfect foundation.
Whether arbitrariness inheritance can be restricted coherently without either reaching divine creation or conflicting with grounding's explanatory role.
Inheritance applies to tight necessitating grounding, not to indeterministic creative explanation, so a free creator need not inherit contingent limits.
The restriction preserves the claim that strongly necessitating essential grounds can inherit arbitrariness.
The distinction does not answer the separate challenge concerning value transmission from necessary conditions.
Whether the inheritance principle illegitimately extends from necessitating grounding to God's contingent creative explanations.
Introducing a deeper divine ground for fixed features such as tripersonality may generate layers in God that conflict with traditional simplicity.
The grounding strategy must explain divine fixed structure without creating a deeper arbitrary layer.
A perfect-foundation model must remain coherent with the theological commitments attached to divine simplicity.
Whether the proposed deeper grounding structure within God remains compatible with traditional divine simplicity and fundamentality.
